text:
Richard Stallman is a prominent advocate for software freedom and the founder of the Free Software Foundation (FSF), a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization established in 1985. He launched the GNU Project in September 1983 to create a free, Unix-compatible operating system, emphasizing that software freedom is a moral necessity rather than merely a pragmatic one. Stallman popularized the concept of "copyleft," first implemented in the GNU Emacs General Public License and later expanded into the GNU General Public License (GPL) in 1989, a legal mechanism designed to protect the rights of users to modify and redistribute software. Key contributions to the GNU system include the development of essential tools such as GNU Emacs (a text editor), the GNU Compiler Collection (GCC), GNU Make, and the GNU Debugger. Although the project lacked a kernel until 1991, when the Linux kernel was added to form the GNU/Linux operating system, Stallman and the FSF maintain that the system should be referred to as GNU/Linux to reflect the GNU project's role as its principal developer.
Stallman's career has been marked by intense activism regarding digital rights management (DRM), copyright reform, and surveillance resistance. He has frequently advocated for reduced copyright terms, the abolition of intellectual property, and civil disobedience against restrictive software practices, such as his "Defective by Design" campaign. His views on free software have occasionally led to controversy, including debates over the definition of "free software" versus "open source," his past comments regarding Jeffrey Epstein, and his stance on child pornography laws, which prompted calls for his resignation from MIT in 2019. Following this backlash, Stallman resigned from his roles at MIT and the FSF board in 2019 but later announced his return to the FSF board in 2021. He remains a vocal critic of proprietary software, encryption on non-secret data, and corporate overreach, while utilizing free software and privacy-preserving technologies in his own daily life.
